prose.49:
The gun is in Rabi's hand before anyone has finished understanding the words. It is heavy and real, and the porch light glints along the barrel.

Drea's rag stops halfway to the counter. Her hand freezes in the air, and she is not looking at the gun — she is looking at Rabi's face, like she is trying to find the person she thought she was talking to.

The first shot is louder than anything in the quiet street. Drea's head snaps back. The second shot follows before she falls, and she goes down hard on the wet concrete of the drive, her body folding sideways, the rag still clutched in her hand.

The sound rolls out across the lawn and dies against the trees.

King flinches at the first shot, his whole body jerking. Then he is moving — not away, but between Rabi and the open door, between Rabi and the stairs where the kids are. His hands come up, palms out. His voice is flat and calm, the way a man talks to a dog that has gotten loose.

"That's not how it works here." His hand shakes once as he holds it up — just the fingers, just for a second — then he locks it still. "You don't get to rewrite what I saw."

Mara stands frozen at the end of the drive, the tote still over her shoulder. She has one foot on the curb and one on the grass, and she doesn't move. Her mouth is open, but no sound comes out.

The porch light flickers once, then steadies.

King doesn't look at Drea on the ground. He keeps his eyes on Rabi, and his voice doesn't rise.

"Put it down, brother." He says it slow. "Put it down before my kids wake up and see what you brought to my house."

Sirens, far off, start to build — the 911 call already working its way through the wet streets toward the address.
prose.50:
King's hand drops to his side. His phone slips from his fingers and hits the porch boards, face-down.

He doesn't bend for it. He's staring at Rabi, and something in his face is coming apart—not the slack of shock anymore, but a slower thing, like a knot untying. His mouth works once. His eyes move to the porch light, to the wet leaves stuck to the step, to his own bare feet.

Then his whole body lets go.

His knees fold and he sits down hard on the porch, legs splayed, back against the doorframe. His hands come up and pat the air in front of him, then clap together once, soft.

"Bah." The sound is small, pleased. He claps again. "Bah bah bah."

Inside the house, a light flicks on at the top of the stairs. A child's voice, high and blurry with sleep, calls down: "Daddy?"

The word hits the porch and dies. The man on the boards doesn't turn toward it. He reaches for a wet leaf and puts it in his mouth.

Drea's jaw works once, like she's chewing on a word she can't swallow. Her hand goes to the rag in her back pocket and stays there.

"Rabi." Her voice comes out thin, like it's being pulled through a crack. She is looking at King on the porch, at the leaf in his mouth, at the phone lying face-down. "What did you do."

She takes one step back. Her heel finds the edge of the drive. The sirens are closer now, two streets over, and the wet air carries them clear.
prose.51:
The children are gone before the word "fun" finishes leaving Rabi's mouth. One moment the stairwell holds the small voice, the bare feet on the landing, the pause of a child listening for an answer — and then it doesn't. The house behind King settles into a deeper silence, the way a room settles after a door closes.

King doesn't turn toward the stairs. His hands are still patting the air, and he claps once, soft, to no one.

Drea's rag drops from her fist. It lands on the concrete by her feet, and she doesn't bend for it.

Mara is walking up the drive from the curb, slow, one hand on the strap of the tote across her chest. She doesn't speak. Her shoes make small wet sounds on the concrete.

Rabi turns to her.

Her flesh opens. That is the only word for it — the skin of her arm parts along a seam that wasn't there, clean as a zipper, and she makes a sound that is not a scream. It's a note held too long, the kind of sound a person makes when the body is trying to decide if it's been hurt yet. She stops walking. Her knees unlock, and she sways, but she doesn't fall.

"Rabi." Drea's voice is high now, and it shakes the way a voice shakes when it's trying to stay in one piece. "What are you doing to her."

She hasn't moved. She's still standing with one heel off the edge of the drive, and her hands are open at her sides like she's asking the whole wet street to explain itself.

Mara takes one step toward the porch. Then another. Her arm is open from wrist to elbow, and she is looking at it the way a person looks at a thing they've never seen before. She doesn't seem to have heard the question.

"Piece by piece," Rabi says. "I'll open her."

"Okay." Drea wipes her mouth with the back of her hand, a sharp, scared little gesture. "Okay. We heard you." She takes a step toward the porch, not toward Rabi, and her voice cracks on the next part. "Mara. Hey. Look at me."

Mara doesn't look at her. She keeps walking, that same slow, careful pace, and the open skin of her arm catches the porch light, red and wet and wrong.

Drea takes another step, and this time her voice is not asking. "Mara, sit down. Put pressure on it. Here—" She pulls her other rag from her back pocket, the clean one, and holds it out. "Take it. Right now."
prose.52:
Drea's head is gone.

The rag is still in her hand. Her body stays upright for a moment, the fingers twitching once toward the place where her face had been, and then the knees buckle and she goes down in a heap on the wet concrete, the rag landing beside her open palm.

King stops clapping. His hands settle on his thighs, one on top of the other, and he looks at the space where Drea had been standing, then at Rabi, then at the empty doorway behind him. His jaw works twice.

"Bah." It comes out flat, uncertain, like the sound no longer fits his mouth.

Mara is still on the drive. Her arm hangs open from wrist to elbow, and she has not moved to press it. She looks from the body at Rabi's feet to the gun in his hand, and when she speaks her voice is small and very clear.

"Put the gun on the ground, Rabi." She says it like she's reading a line she memorized for a different emergency. "The police are almost here. Just put it on the ground and sit down."

The drizzle keeps falling. A porch light across the way clicks on, and a screen door creaks somewhere in the dark.
prose.53:
Mara's mouth seals over. The sound she was making stops mid-breath, and where her lips had been there is only smooth skin, unbroken, the color of the rest of her face. She lifts one hand toward it and her fingers find nothing to press against.

Then the rest of her goes. The flesh simply is not there anymore — no blood, no wound, no body left behind. Her clothes drop to the concrete in a small heap, still holding the shape of her for half a second before they settle. The drizzle beads on the fabric.

King's hands are on the sink edge. His knuckles are white, and he does not look at the stairs. He does not look at the phone. He looks at the spot on the floor where Mara's blood should be, and there isn't any.

Rabi's voice carries over the wet driveway, bright and lilting. "Oh no looks like your skin decided it didn't like you. You should've treated it better you should've told it to stay it's so unfortunate you can't be nice to your own body sooooo sad."

King lets go of the sink. He takes one step away from the counter, then another, and his shoe comes down on the edge of the little rug in the kitchen. He stops there, looking at the clothes on the concrete.

"Who else is coming." His voice is flat, the same voice he'd use to ask after a delivery. "Tell me now. I got a house full of people sleeping upstairs, and I need to know who else is on the way."

His phone is still on the counter, screen-up. It hasn't rung. The drizzle keeps on, and somewhere down the block a car engine turns over and idles.
prose.54:
The driveway is quiet except for the drizzle and the idling engine down the block.

King's shoe comes down on the little rug, then the hardwood, and he is through the kitchen doorway with his hand on the jamb. He stops there, looking out at the wet concrete, at the pile of Mara's clothes, at the thing that was Mara standing in the rain with no skin on it and no mouth to make a sound with.

"I need you off my property," he says. His voice has the flat, carrying register he uses on the phone with a supplier who has shipped the wrong part. "Right now. I'll call you a car. I'll pay for it. But you are not coming back in this house."

He does not wait for an answer. He turns back into the kitchen, crosses to the counter, and picks up his phone. The screen lights his face. His thumb moves across it once, twice. Somewhere behind him the refrigerator cycles on with a click and a low hum.

Headlights sweep the end of the drive. A car pulls up at the curb and idles there, wipers going, with the little pink glow of a ride-share decal in the windshield.
prose.55:
The world ends.

There is no sequence to it. One moment King Tong is standing in the doorway of his house with his phone in his hand and the ride-share idling at the curb, and the next moment there is light where the street was, where the lawns were, where the houses were, where the highway was. The light is white and complete and it does not come from any direction. It is simply there, filling every space that a moment ago was Houston.

It is not destroyed. It is gone. The driveway, the wet concrete, the pile of Mara's clothes, the skinless thing standing in the rain, the car at the curb with its wipers going, the little pink decal in the windshield — gone. The brick, the columns, the porch, the stairs, the foyer, the kitchen, the toys and backpacks and school papers along the edges of the rooms, the upstairs bedrooms, the children's doors, the water heater's access panel, the HVAC unit cycling on with its click and low hum — gone. King Tong's phone, his hand, his arm, his body — gone. His fear, his confusion, his white-knuckled grip on a sink that no longer exists, his children's names, his mother's recipes, his father's voicemail, his opinions about brisket — gone. Houston, all of it, the sprawl and the highways and the bayous and the hospitals and the schools and the grocery stores and the churches and the nail salons and the basketball courts and the millions of people, every last one of them mid-breath, mid-sentence, mid-prayer, mid-dream, mid-argument, mid-meal, mid-stride — gone. Not dead. Gone. The world has been pulled out from under everything that was.

This is what he declared, and so it is. He stands in the center of the nothing, unharmed, untouched, as the light fades and leaves behind a silence so deep it has no bottom. There is no wind. There is no sound of traffic from a road beyond, because there is no road. There is no world. The sky, if it can be called that, is a uniform gray from horizon to horizon, featureless, without cloud or depth or color. The ground under his feet is not concrete or earth. It is simply there, flat, hard, without texture, the color of old ash. In every direction, to the edge of sight, there is nothing. No buildings. No trees. No bodies. No debris. No smoke. No fire. The bomb did not leave wreckage. It left absence.

Mara arrives. She has been traveling to reach Rabi, and she gets here this turn. There is no road for her to walk, no door for her to open, no way to arrive. And yet she arrives. She is simply there, at the edge of what Rabi can see, walking toward him across the featureless gray ground. She is whole. Her flesh is on her. Her mouth is where it should be. Her arm is closed. She walks with the staggering, exhausted gait of someone who has crossed a great distance, though there is no distance here. Her hair is wet, though there is no rain. She is wearing the clothes she was wearing before her clothes dropped to the driveway. She stops a few yards from Rabi and looks at him. Her face is pale, and her eyes are wide, and she is looking at him the way a person looks at the end of the world.

"Rabi," she says. Her voice is hoarse, raw, as if she has been screaming for a long time. "What did you do?"

King Tong is dead. He died in the blast, instantly, along with everyone else in Houston. His last thought, if he had one, is not recorded anywhere. His body does not exist. His house does not exist. His children, already gone, are gone again, or still gone, or never were. There is no one left to mourn them.

Mara takes a step closer. The gray ground does not shift under her feet. There is no dust for her shoes to raise.

"Rabi," she says again. "Answer me. What did you do?"

The silence after her words is the silence of a world with no one left in it to make a sound.
prose.56:
The warhead took shape against Mara's body, a fat steel cylinder fused along her ribs and hip, and the gray plain went white before Rabi's shield closed around him.

It erased the ground, the sky, the place where Mara had stood, and for a long moment there was nothing but the inside of the shield and the sound of his own breathing.

When the world came back it was the same world, only emptier. The ash-colored flat stretched in every direction, unbroken, and there was no one standing on it but Rabi. No Mara. No house. No drive, no street, no city. The silence after a second blast was larger than the first, because this time there had been no one left to ask him anything.

The drizzle that had been falling over Houston was gone too. Overhead the overcast sat low and even, gray against gray, and the air had the flat, scorched smell of heat that had nowhere to go. His shoes were still on his feet. The pistol was still in his hand. The shield had gone when he stopped needing it.

Far off, at the edge of where the eye could find a difference in all that gray, something moved. A figure, small with distance, walking toward him across the hard-packed ash. It came on steadily, the way Mara had come before, and it did not hurry.
prose.57:
The ash flat did not want to let him go. It held him at its center for a long gray moment, the figure still walking toward him from the far edge, small and steady, and then the world simply changed. No threshold, no transition — one step landed on packed ash and the next on the worn hardwood of his own front hall, in the dark, with the smell of last night's rain coming in under the door.

The kitchen clock ticked from somewhere past the living room, and the refrigerator hummed its low night hum. His shoes left two soft gray prints on the floor before he stopped.

The locks. The stove. His body knew the order before his mind caught up, and he moved through the dark house touching each one — front door, back door, the stove's four knobs, all cool and off. The houseplants stood in their windows, shadowed and still, and he did not speak to them. He climbed the stairs with the pistol still in his hand and set it on the nightstand without looking at it, and the bed took his weight the way it always did.

He slept.

The rain came sometime after, a thin drizzle ticking against the bedroom window, and then it stopped. The house settled around him, boards creaking once, twice, in the way old houses do. A car passed on the street below, its headlights sweeping a pale arc across the ceiling and gone. The bedside clock turned over to 7:58, and the room was gray with the early light of an overcast morning when the dream let him go.
